summary: A heat pump can very likely heat this house, but whether the existing radiators are big enough is still open. One side photo of a radiator would settle most of it.

thresholds.result: yellow: needs 55-60 C, higher running cost
needs > 60 C: some radiators should be upgraded

boundaries.how: Side photo of a typical radiator plus its height and width

reasons.text: Two-pipe system: all radiators get water at the same temperature.
Radiator type unknown: the house runs with Type 33 at about 50-53 C, with Type 22 at about 58-62 C, with Type 11 at about 77-84 C.
12 radiator valves need replacement anyway; a good moment for hydraulic balancing.
79-92 W/m2 is above 75 W/m2: better windows or insulation may be worth it.

homeowner_can_provide: Side photo of one typical radiator, plus its height and width
Current flow temperature setting of the boiler, if known
technician_checks: Outdoor unit placement, sound and permits
assumptions: Unheated area of unknown size (top floor, size unknown): heated area 70-100 % of floor area
Partially renovated, built before 1979: 80-120 W/m2 (no official row for 'partially')
Full-load hours 1800-2100 h (official approx. 2,000; range ours)
Radiator size unknown: assumed 600 x 1000 mm
Radiator output vs temperature: EN 442, n = 1.3, 10 K spread
Heat pump also covers hot water, at the same JAZ as space heating
